deep.reconstruction:
This page (MS p. 17, folio 13r) contains no computation. It is the fair-copy manuscript of the historical section (§2) of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Ueber die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867). It continues the previous page's summary of Dirichlet's 1829 Crelle paper.

(a) Completing the sentence from the previous page. Take a 2π-periodic f that (1) is integrable throughout and (2) has finitely many maxima and minima, but (3) at some jump x0 has f(x0) ≠ (f(x0+0)+f(x0-0))/2. Such an f 'obviously' cannot be represented by a trigonometric series. Riemann's reason: the series that represents f away from the discontinuities is, by Dirichlet's theorem, the Fourier series S(x) = a0/2 + Σ (a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx), with a_n = (1/π)∫ f(t) cos nt dt (similarly b_n). At x0 that series converges to (f(x0+0)+f(x0-0))/2 ≠ f(x0).

Implicit step (mine): this tacitly assumes that a trigonometric series agreeing with f off the jumps must be the Fourier series of f. That is a uniqueness statement that Riemann's own later sections and Cantor (1870) address. Read strictly, the remark means 'the Dirichlet representation fails there'.

(b) The question of whether and when a function violating conditions (1) or (2) is representable remains undecided by Dirichlet's investigation.

(c) Historical assessment.
- Dirichlet's work gave a firm foundation to many analytic investigations.
- By clarifying where Euler erred, he settled a question that had occupied excellent mathematicians for more than seventy years, since 1753 (Daniel Bernoulli's vibrating-string paper and the ensuing controversy with Euler and d'Alembert).
- For all cases occurring in nature the question is settled, since functions outside Dirichlet's hypotheses do not occur in nature.

(d) Motivation, continued on the next page. The unsettled cases nevertheless deserve attention for two reasons.
- First (as Dirichlet himself remarked at the end of his paper), the topic is closely tied to the principles of the infinitesimal calculus and can bring them to greater clarity and definiteness.
- The second reason (number theory) follows on p. 18.
errors: No mathematical errors. The date arithmetic is consistent: 1753 to 1829 is 76 years, i.e. 'more than seventy'.

The claim that a function violating condition 3 'obviously' cannot be represented quietly relies on uniqueness of the representing series, which was not yet proven. This is a gap in rigor rather than an error, and it is standard for the time.
'Functions outside Dirichlet's scope do not occur in nature' is a physical or philosophical judgment, not a mathematical claim.

results.what: Dirichlet's sufficient conditions (integrable, finitely many extrema, mean value at jumps) for representability by a Fourier series, and the observation that violating the mean-value condition prevents representation
results.modern_name: Dirichlet conditions / Dirichlet-Jordan convergence theorem (convergence to the average of the one-sided limits at a jump)

results.what: Historical account of the vibrating-string controversy since 1753 and of Euler's error, plus motivation for studying non-Dirichlet functions

deep.surprise_reason: This is the manuscript of the well-known, published historical section of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift. The wording matches the printed text essentially verbatim, and it contains no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: The Fourier series of the square wave sign(x) on (-pi,pi) takes the value 0 = (1+(-1))/2 at the jump x=0. This is the mean of the one-sided limits, illustrating condition 3.
Dirichlet kernel identity 1+2*sum_{k=1}^n cos(kt) = sin((2n+1)t/2)/sin(t/2) for n=5; it should be numerically 0. This underlies the integral discussed on the previous page.
Dirichlet's 1829 paper came more than seventy years after 1753, as stated.

transcription_corrections: 'Unstetigkeitsstellen[?]' should read 'Unstetigkeitsstellen' (consistent with the printed 1867 text: 'würde in den Unstetigkeitsstellen selbst von ihr abweichen').
The isolated '13' is the archival folio number written in the margin, not part of the text; '17.' at top is Riemann's page number.
